course.title: Economics: Markets and Strategy
course.description: Price a trade-off, find where supply meets demand, weigh a tax and outguess a rival. Every idea is worked with real numbers.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with basic algebra: solving two linear equations and finding the area of a triangle. No previous economics is assumed; the depth matches a strong first-year university microeconomics course.

lessons.title: What it really costs

steps.headline: A choice costs whatever you could best have done instead.

lead.text: Your £10 ticket also cost you sandwiches. Money, time and attention can each be used once, so every choice uses up something that could have gone elsewhere.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up. Only the best one counts, not every option you passed over.
Workshop A spends one week making chairs or tables. Every table takes the same slice of the week, so the swap between the two happens at one steady rate.

reveal.text: You just priced a table in chairs: 60 ÷ 20 = 3. That price, the chairs given up for each table, is its opportunity cost.

steps.headline: A frontier shows the most of one good you can have for each amount of the other.

lead.text: Plot every mix that uses Workshop A's whole week and you get a line, the production possibilities frontier. On it, all the time is used. Inside it, time is left idle. Beyond it, you would need more time than the week holds.

steps.headline: A country makes food and machines. Moving from 40 to 60 food, what does each extra unit of food cost?

workedSteps.text: Read the frontier. At 40 food it sits at 70 machines; at 60 food it sits at 40.
Find the machines given up.
Find the food gained.
Share the loss across the gain.

lead.text: Now price the next step along the same frontier. An average over the whole frontier hides how the cost changes from step to step.

reveal.text: This step cost 2 machines per unit of food; the step before it cost 1.5. The price of food is rising.

steps.headline: Opportunity cost usually rises as you make more of one good.

lead.text: The first food comes from farmland and workers who were never much use in a factory, so few machines are lost. Later food pulls engineers and factory sites onto farms. The cost climbs, and the frontier bows outward. A straight one means every resource suits both goods equally.
Not every trade-off bends. Priya splits her study time between essays and problem sets, and each task takes a fixed time. Her trade-off is a straight line.

lessons.orientation: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You have £30 for the day, and a sandwich costs £5.

intro.promise: By the end you'll price a choice by what it gives up, and read that price off a frontier.

recap.keyIdea: A choice costs the best alternative you give up. Along a frontier that cost is the machines lost per unit of food gained, and it usually rises.

blocks.text: You priced a table at 3 chairs and a cinema ticket at 2 sandwiches. Then you found the cost of food rising from 1.5 to 2 machines per unit.

recap.nextHook: If two people face different costs for the same job, who should do which?

lessons.title: Who should make what

lead.text: Ana makes more cakes and more loaves than Ben in a day. Faster at both, so does she get to bake everything? Compare what each baker gives up for one cake.

reveal.text: You compared opportunity costs. A cake costs Ben 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves and Ana 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so the quicker baker is the dearer one.

steps.headline: Whoever gives up less has the comparative advantage.

lead.text: Ana has an absolute advantage in both goods: she makes more of each. That does not settle who should bake what.
Comparative advantage belongs to whoever has the lower opportunity cost. Two producers with different cost ratios each hold one.

steps.headline: Ana bakes 12 loaves or 6 cakes a day; Ben bakes 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who should bake what?

workedSteps.text: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Price a loaf in cakes for each baker.
Give each job to the lower cost: Ben bakes the cakes, Ana bakes the loaves.

steps.headline: Ben bakes only cakes and swaps 2 of them with Ana at 1.75 loaves each. Does he come out ahead?

workedSteps.text: Before the swap Ben splits his day, so he makes 2 cakes and 3 loaves.
Now he bakes 4 cakes, keeps 2 and swaps 2 away.
Find the loaves he receives.
Compare with the 3 loaves he used to bake.

steps.headline: Both sides gain at any price between their two opportunity costs.

lead.text: A buyer gains if the price is below what making the good would cost them. A seller gains if it is above what making it costs them. Any price in between helps both.
Mira and Tom share a studio. Start with Tom: what does he give up for each page he codes?

reveal.text: Tom gives up 4 reports per page and Mira only 2, so Mira has the comparative advantage in pages.

lead.text: Cara is twice as productive as Dan at both jobs. That is a large absolute advantage. Check whether it makes trade worthwhile.

reveal.text: Equal costs leave no price that helps both sides. Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not differences in productivity.

lessons.orientation: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes in a day, but not both. She is quicker than Ben at everything.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say who should make what, and show that trade can leave both sides better off.

recap.keyIdea: Comparative advantage belongs to whoever gives up less. Specialise where your cost is lower and trade at a price between the two costs, and both sides gain.

blocks.text: You found that Ben's cakes cost 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2, and that Ben ended half a loaf better off. When Cara and Dan both gave up 2 loaves per cake, trade offered nothing.

recap.nextHook: Costs are not just totals. Next: the cost of one more.

lessons.title: The next unit

steps.headline: Decide one extra unit at a time: is the next one worth its cost?

lead.text: Marginal means one more. A choice about how much to do is a string of small choices. Marginal benefit is what the extra unit adds. Marginal cost is what it adds to your costs.
Keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost. Stop when it falls below it.
A café is deciding how many late hours to open. Each extra hour brings in less than the one before, and costs more in staff time. Decide hour by hour.

reveal.text: You compared each hour's own benefit with its own cost and stopped where an hour stopped paying. The best choice sits where marginal benefit meets marginal cost.

steps.headline: A bookshop's late hours bring £80, £60, £40 and £20, and each costs £30 to open. How many should it open, and what does it gain?

workedSteps.text: Find each hour's net gain: benefit minus cost.
Open every hour whose net gain is positive: the first three.
Add their gains.

steps.headline: The café opens its first three late hours. What total net benefit does it gain?

workedSteps.text: Hour 1: benefit £90, cost £30.
Hour 2: benefit £70, cost £35. Find its net benefit.
Hour 3: benefit £55, cost £45.
Add the three net benefits.

steps.headline: A cost you cannot get back should not change the decision.

lead.text: Some costs are paid already, whatever you decide next. A non-refundable concert ticket is one.
Such a cost is called a sunk cost. It is the same under every option, so it cannot change a comparison between options.
Now staffing gets dearer: every hour costs £20 more than before. Decide again, hour by hour.

reveal.text: Dearer hours moved the stopping point from the third hour to the second. When marginal cost rises, the best amount falls.

lead.text: A manager notes that the first four hours average £63.75 of benefit each, well above the £50 cost of the fourth. She says to open it. Test her reasoning on the fourth hour alone.

reveal.text: The average includes hours that are being opened anyway. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide the extra hour.

lessons.orientation: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are at a pizza counter. Each extra slice is worth a little less to you than the one before.

intro.promise: By the end you'll decide how much to do by comparing the next unit's benefit with its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

recap.keyIdea: Decide one extra unit at a time. Keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

blocks.text: You bought four slices and opened three late hours. When costs rose, the café opened only two. The fourth hour would lose £10 although the average looked good.

recap.nextHook: You can now say how much one buyer wants. Next: how buyers and sellers together set a price.

lessons.title: Demand meets supply

steps.headline: A demand curve says how much buyers plan to buy at each price.

lead.text: Higher price, fewer cups: that is the law of demand. As an equation, Qd = 100 − 2P, where Q is cups a day and P is the price in pounds. Qd is the quantity demanded, with everything else held constant.
The stall's demand is Qd = 100 − 2P. Put a price in and the equation gives the cups buyers plan to take.

reveal.text: You turned a price into a quantity, which is what the demand equation does. At £15 buyers plan 70 cups; at £30 they would plan only 40.

steps.headline: The market settles where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

lead.text: Sellers offer more at a higher price. Here supply is Qs = 4P − 20. Equilibrium is the price where Qd equals Qs: every cup offered finds a buyer, and no willing buyer goes without.

steps.headline: Bagels: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10. Find the equilibrium price.

workedSteps.text: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.
Collect the P terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Divide both sides by 5.
Check that both equations agree at that price.

steps.headline: Coffee: Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. Find the equilibrium price and the cups traded.

workedSteps.text: Set Qd equal to Qs.
Collect terms.
Solve for the price.
Put the price into the demand equation to find the cups traded.

lead.text: Now a market with its own numbers. Set the two quantities equal and solve for the price.

reveal.text: Same moves as the bagels and the coffee: equate, collect, divide. At £12 buyers want 32 and sellers offer 32.

lead.text: A café fixes its coffee price at £25, above the price where plans match. See what that does to the cups offered and the cups people want.

reveal.text: At £25 sellers offer 80 cups and buyers want only 50: a surplus of 30. Unsold stock pushes sellers to cut the price. At £15 the reverse holds, a shortage of 30.

lessons.orientation: Read linear demand and supply equations and solve them for the equilibrium price and quantity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A coffee stall finds that every £1 it adds to the price loses it the same number of customers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read demand and supply equations and solve them for the price where a market settles.

recap.keyIdea: Equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Set the equations equal, solve for the price, then substitute it back to find the quantity.

blocks.text: You found £20 and 60 cups for coffee and £12 for the market in the try. You saw that a price stuck at £25 leaves 30 cups unsold.

recap.nextHook: What happens to the equilibrium when something changes demand or supply?

lessons.title: When the curves move

steps.headline: A price change moves you along a curve; anything else shifts the curve.

lead.text: Price is on the axis of the demand curve. So a change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve. Change anything else and the whole curve moves: a shift.
“Demand” names the whole curve. “Quantity demanded” is one point on it.

steps.headline: Anything but the good's own price can shift demand or supply.

lead.text: Demand shifts with income, tastes, expectations, the number of buyers and the prices of related goods. Supply shifts with input costs, technology and the number of sellers. A shift right means more at every price.
Substitutes replace each other, like tea and coffee. A rise in one's price lifts demand for the other.

steps.headline: Incomes fall and buyers want 30 fewer cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium for Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20.

workedSteps.text: Demand shifts left by 30 cups at every price.
Supply is untouched. Set the new demand equal to it.
Collect terms.
Solve for the price, then the quantity.

steps.headline: Incomes rise and buyers want 30 more cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Demand shifts right.
Set it equal to the unchanged supply.
Solve for the price.
Find the quantity.

lead.text: Now a frost hits the harvest. A cause on the supply side moves the supply curve, and demand stays where it was.

reveal.text: Supply shifted left: the price rose from £20 to £24 and the quantity fell from 60 to 52. You solved it the same way as a demand shift.

lead.text: Now demand and supply each grow by the same number of cups at every price. Write both new equations and solve them together.

reveal.text: Quantity rose from 60 to 90 but the price stayed at £20. When both curves shift right, quantity must rise; the price depends on which shift is larger.

lessons.orientation: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A coffee market has settled at £20 and 60 cups a day. Then a fad for coffee arrives.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a movement along a curve from a shift of it, and solve for the new equilibrium.

recap.keyIdea: A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. Anything else shifts the curve, and you find the new equilibrium by solving again with the new equation.

blocks.text: You found a shortage of 12 cups after a fad, then £15 when incomes fell and £25 when they rose. A frost lifted the price to £24; shifting both curves together left it unchanged.

recap.nextHook: A price change moves quantity, but by how much? Next: how sensitive buyers are.

lessons.title: How strongly buyers respond

steps.headline: Elasticity compares how far quantity moves with how far price moved.

lead.text: Price elasticity of demand divides the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price. Each percentage uses the average of the two values as its base: the midpoint method.
Above 1, demand is elastic. Below 1, it is inelastic.

steps.headline: A gym's price rises from £4 to £6 a visit and visits fall from 130 to 70 a day. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: Quantity change as a share of the average quantity.
Price change as a share of the average price.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
Above 1, so demand is elastic.

steps.headline: A bus pass falls from £6 to £4 and passes sold rise from 95 to 105. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: The average quantity is 100 and the quantity changes by 10.
The average price is £5 and the price changes by £2.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.

lead.text: Same method, a different market. Average first, then divide the two percentage changes.

reveal.text: Elasticity of 3 is well above 1: demand for tickets is elastic, so buyers respond more than in proportion.

steps.headline: Elastic demand: a price cut raises revenue. Inelastic demand: it lowers it.

lead.text: Revenue is price times quantity. A price cut shrinks the first and grows the second. If quantity grows by a bigger percentage than price fell, revenue rises. If it grows by less, revenue falls.
Back to the concert: the price fell from £11 to £9 and sales rose from 35 to 65. Work out the revenue at each price.

reveal.text: Revenue rose from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, as the rule says for elastic demand.

lead.text: A straight demand line has a different elasticity at each price. Test a museum, with demand Qd = 200 − 10P, as its entry price falls.

reveal.text: Revenue is £990 at both prices, so elasticity here is exactly 1. On a straight line demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones, and revenue peaks where it equals 1.

lessons.orientation: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A food stall wonders whether a lower price will bring in more money.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how strongly buyers respond to price, and say what a price change does to revenue.

recap.keyIdea: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity over the percentage change in price, taken at the midpoint. Elastic demand means a price cut raises revenue; inelastic demand means it lowers it.

blocks.text: You measured 1.5 for gym visits, 0.25 for bus passes and 3 for concert tickets. At the museum, revenue stayed at £990 when elasticity was exactly 1.

recap.nextHook: Elasticity shows how buyers react. Next: what buyers and sellers gain from a trade.

lessons.title: Who gains from a sale

steps.headline: Surplus is the gap between a limit and the price actually paid.

lead.text: Each point on the demand curve is the most some buyer would pay: their willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is that amount minus the price paid. Producer surplus is the seller's version: the price received minus the lowest price they would accept.
Take one buyer in the coffee market, where every cup sells at the same market price.

reveal.text: The gap is value she kept: her consumer surplus. Add up every buyer's gap and you get an area on the diagram.

steps.headline: Bagels: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10. Find consumer surplus.

workedSteps.text: Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
Find the price at which demand reaches zero.
The base is the quantity sold; the height is the gap between that price and the market price.
Take half of base times height.

steps.headline: Coffee sells 60 cups at £20, with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. Find both surpluses.

workedSteps.text: Demand reaches zero at £50, so the buyers' height is the gap above the price.
Half of base times height gives consumer surplus.
Supply starts at £5, so the sellers' height is the gap below the price.
Half of base times height gives producer surplus.

lead.text: A different market, the same triangle. Find the market price first.

reveal.text: Same moves: equilibrium, the price where demand reaches zero, then half of base times height.

steps.headline: Free exchange at equilibrium makes total surplus as large as it can be.

lead.text: Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus. A cup adds to it when its buyer values it above its cost to make. Equilibrium trades every such cup and no other.
Now a rule caps coffee sales below the free-market quantity. The cups that can no longer be sold are the ones to look at.

reveal.text: The lost value is the triangle of base 20 and height 15: £150 of deadweight loss, surplus that nobody gets.

lessons.orientation: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Three friends each have a limit on what they would pay for a concert ticket.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure who gains from a sale as areas on the diagram, and show why equilibrium makes the total largest.

recap.keyIdea: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would pay and the price. Producer surplus is the gap between the price and what sellers would accept. Equilibrium makes their total as large as possible.

blocks.text: You found £900 of consumer surplus and £450 of producer surplus in the coffee market. Capping sales at 40 cups wasted £150 of it.

recap.nextHook: What happens to that surplus when a tax drives a wedge between buyers and sellers?

lessons.title: What a tax takes

steps.headline: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers keep.

lead.text: Sellers hand the tax to the government on every unit, so what they keep is the buyers' price minus the tax. They decide how much to supply from what they keep. To find the new equilibrium, put P − tax in place of P in the supply equation.
Coffee sellers must hand over £6 on every cup. Their supply now depends on the price they keep, which is the buyers' price minus 6.

reveal.text: You found that buyers pay £24 and sellers keep £18. The £6 tax is shared: £4 to buyers and £2 to sellers.

steps.headline: Demand is Qd = 60 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P − 20. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. Find the buyers' price, the quantity and the revenue.

workedSteps.text: Sellers keep P − 4, so supply in terms of the buyers' price changes.
Set it equal to demand.
Collect terms and solve.
Find the quantity, then the revenue.

steps.headline: A tax raises revenue on the units still sold and destroys surplus on the rest.

lead.text: Tax revenue is the tax per unit times the units still sold. The trades the tax stops were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers. That lost surplus is a triangle called deadweight loss: half of the tax times the fall in quantity.

steps.headline: With the £6 tax, coffee sales fall from 60 to 52 cups a day. Find the revenue and the lost surplus.

workedSteps.text: Tax per cup times the cups still sold gives the revenue.
Cups no longer sold.
Half of the tax times that fall gives the deadweight loss.

lead.text: A new market, the same moves: find the buyers' price with the tax, then the quantity.

reveal.text: Trade fell below its old level, as it does with any per-unit tax. The units that vanished are where the deadweight loss sits.

lead.text: Now gym passes, where buyers are more price-sensitive than sellers. The same £6 tax is collected from sellers. Compare what happens to the price buyers pay.

reveal.text: Buyers' price rises from £25 to £27: they bear £2 of the £6, against £4 in the coffee market. The side that can more easily walk away bears less.

lessons.orientation: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A £6 tax on every cup of coffee is collected from the sellers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the price and quantity after a per-unit tax, and say who bears it and what it destroys.

recap.keyIdea: A per-unit tax splits the price into what buyers pay and what sellers keep. It raises revenue on units still sold, destroys surplus on units that stop trading, and falls more on the side that finds it harder to walk away.

blocks.text: You found buyers paying £24 and sellers keeping £18, £312 of revenue and £24 of lost surplus. In the gym market buyers carried only £2 of the £6.

recap.nextHook: Taxes are one way to change a market. Next: price controls, and costs that fall on people outside the trade.

lessons.title: Controls and spillovers

steps.headline: A price control only matters if it stops the market price being reached.

lead.text: A ceiling is a legal maximum price. A floor is a legal minimum. A ceiling below equilibrium binds: buyers want more than sellers offer, a shortage. A floor above equilibrium binds too: sellers offer more than buyers take, a surplus. Set the other way round, a control does nothing.
In the coffee market a ceiling of £12 sits below the equilibrium price. Compare what buyers want with what sellers offer at £12.

reveal.text: You compared the two quantities at the controlled price. Only 28 cups change hands, fewer than the 60 at equilibrium, so queues and connections ration the cups instead of price.

steps.headline: Coffee has Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. A floor of £26 is set. How many cups go unsold?

workedSteps.text: Compare the floor with the equilibrium price of £20. It sits above, so it binds.
Find the cups buyers want at £26.
Find the cups sellers offer at £26.
Subtract.

steps.headline: The floor is raised to £30. How many cups go unsold?

workedSteps.text: £30 is above the equilibrium price, so the floor binds.
Find the cups sellers offer at £30.
Find the cups buyers want at £30.
Subtract demand from supply.

steps.headline: A cost that lands on other people is missed by the market.

lead.text: When making paint pollutes the neighbours, firms count only their own costs. That unpaid damage is an external cost. To count it, add it to each tonne's cost: replace P with P − damage in the supply equation. A tax equal to the damage makes firms face it, and is called a Pigouvian tax.
Paint firms' own costs give Qs = 4P − 20, and each tonne does £9 of damage. Add the damage to supply, then meet demand.

reveal.text: Counting the damage lifts the cost curve by £9. Social supply meets demand at £26 and 48 tonnes, 12 fewer than the market makes.

lead.text: The market makes 60 tonnes, not 48. A tax of £9 a tonne, equal to the damage, would remove the problem. First measure what the problem costs.

reveal.text: On the 12 extra tonnes the gap between social cost and buyers' value grows from nothing at 48 to £9 at 60: a triangle of £54.

lessons.orientation: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A city caps ticket prices for a sold-out concert.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct a cost that falls on other people.

recap.keyIdea: A control that binds stops buyers and sellers trading as they want: a ceiling creates a shortage, a floor a surplus. A cost that falls on others makes a market overproduce, and a tax equal to the damage corrects it.

blocks.text: You found a shortage of 48 cups under a £12 ceiling and 60 unsold under a £30 floor. The paint market overproduced by 12 tonnes, a loss of £54.

recap.nextHook: So far costs were given. Next: where a firm's costs come from, and how they set its output.

lessons.title: Costs and the best output

steps.headline: Average cost and marginal cost answer different questions.

lead.text: Fixed cost, such as rent, is paid whatever the output. Variable cost grows with output. Their sum is total cost. Average total cost is total cost per unit. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit.
A workshop pays £100 rent whatever it makes. Making q units adds q² in other costs, rising faster as the room fills. Find the cost per unit at 5 units.

reveal.text: You divided total cost by output. Rent spread over more units pulls the average down; crowding costs push it back up.

steps.headline: A workshop pays £400 rent, with variable cost q². At what output is average total cost lowest?

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.
Average cost is lowest where marginal cost meets it.
Take q from both sides.
Solve.

steps.headline: With £100 rent and variable cost q², find the output where average total cost is lowest.

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.
Set them equal and simplify.
Solve for the output.
Put that output into ATC.

steps.headline: A firm should keep producing while the next unit adds more revenue than cost.

lead.text: A competitive firm is a price-taker: the market sets its price. Every extra unit adds that price to revenue, its marginal revenue. So the firm should produce until marginal cost rises to meet the price.
This firm has marginal cost MC = 2q and sells at £30. Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.

reveal.text: Below 15 units the next unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond 15 it adds less. That is the marginal rule from the start of the course, applied to output.

lead.text: The market price falls to £16. Find the best output again, and then see whether it still pays.

reveal.text: A loss of £36 is still better than shutting down, which would lose the whole £100 of rent. In the short run the firm keeps producing.

lessons.orientation: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bakery pays the same rent whether it bakes ten loaves or a hundred.

intro.promise: By the end you'll separate fixed, average and marginal cost, and pick the output that makes a price-taking firm the most profit.

recap.keyIdea: Average total cost is the cost per unit; marginal cost is the cost of one more. A price-taking firm makes the most profit where price equals marginal cost.

blocks.text: You found the lowest-cost output of 10 units and the profit-maximising 15 units, which earned £125. At £16 the firm lost £36 but still beat shutting down.

lessons.title: One seller

steps.headline: A monopolist's extra sale brings in less than its price.

lead.text: A monopolist is the only seller. To sell one more unit it must cut the price on every unit, so marginal revenue falls below the price. For straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ: the same intercept, falling twice as fast.
Demand is P = 100 − Q, so at 30 units the price is £70. Use the marginal revenue line to see what the next unit is worth.

reveal.text: Marginal revenue is £40 while the price is £70. Each extra unit is worth much less to the seller than the price on the tag.

steps.headline: Demand is P = 120 − 2Q and marginal cost is £40. What output and price maximise the monopolist's profit?

workedSteps.text: Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as demand.
Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
Solve for the output.
Read the price from the demand curve.

steps.headline: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is £20. What output and price maximise profit?

workedSteps.text: Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as demand.
Set it equal to marginal cost and solve.
Read the price from the demand curve.

steps.headline: A monopoly stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost.

lead.text: Competition pushes price down to marginal cost. The monopolist stops earlier, where marginal revenue meets marginal cost, then charges what demand allows. Units beyond that point are worth more to buyers than they cost, yet are never made.
A new demand curve and cost. Write the marginal revenue line first, then set it equal to marginal cost.

reveal.text: You doubled the demand slope to get marginal revenue, then solved. At 12 units the monopolist charges £36.

lead.text: Now compare the monopoly with competition. Count the units that competition would sell and the monopoly does not.

reveal.text: The lost value is a triangle with base 40 and height £40: £800. The monopoly's profit is a transfer from buyers to the firm; the £800 is lost to everyone.

lessons.orientation: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output. Then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.

recap.keyIdea: A monopolist's marginal revenue falls below its price, so it stops where MR meets MC and charges what demand allows. That is less output at a higher price than competition, and the units in between are a deadweight loss.

blocks.text: You found marginal revenue of £40 against a £70 price. The monopoly sold 40 units where competition sold 80, and £800 of value was lost.

lessons.title: Strategic choices

steps.headline: Your best choice depends on what the other player does.

lead.text: A payoff matrix lists every pair of choices and what each player earns. To find your best response, fix your rival's choice and compare your own payoffs. A dominant strategy is a best response to every choice the rival might make.
Alpha's payoffs are in the matrix. For each of Beta's choices, find which price pays Alpha more.

reveal.text: You tested Alpha's best response against both of Beta's choices. When one strategy wins both times it is dominant, and Alpha needs no forecast of Beta.

steps.headline: A Nash equilibrium is an outcome where nobody gains by switching alone.

lead.text: In a Nash equilibrium each player's choice is a best response to the other's, so a lone switch never helps. If it leaves both worse off than another outcome they could reach, the game is a prisoner's dilemma.

steps.headline: Price war: Alpha and Beta each choose High or Low. Find the Nash equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
workedSteps.math: Against High: Low pays 14, High pays 10. Against Low: Low pays 5, High pays 2.

workedSteps.text: Beta's payoffs mirror Alpha's, so Low is Beta's best response as well.
Both play Low, and each earns 5.

steps.headline: Two makers each choose plug standard A or B. Matching on A pays 6 each; matching on B pays 4 each; a mismatch pays nothing. Find the Nash equilibria.

workedSteps.text: At A/A, suppose Maker A switches alone to B while Maker B stays on A.
That is below the 6 A earned, so A/A is an equilibrium. B/B works the same way: a lone switch drops a maker from 4 to nothing.
A mismatched cell is not an equilibrium: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.
Count the cells where neither maker gains by switching alone.

lead.text: Back in the price war, both firms play their dominant strategy. Look up what each earns there and add the two together.

reveal.text: Both choose Low and earn £5m each, £10m together, though High/High would give £20m. Each firm's best choice leaves both worse off: a prisoner's dilemma.

lead.text: Now the same firms meet for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat: High first, then it copies Beta's last move. Beta always sets Low.

reveal.text: Alpha is undercut once, then matches Low: £22m, while Beta earns £34m. Against another tit-for-tat player Alpha would earn £10m a round. When a game repeats, the threat of retaliation can make cooperation pay.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week, trading one for the other at a constant rate. How many chairs does each extra table cost?
hints: Both maximums use the same week of work.
Ask how many chairs one table's share of the week could have made.
Divide the maximum number of chairs by the maximum number of tables.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 chairs ÷ 20 tables = 3 chairs per table.

questions.onCorrect: 3 chairs. A table's opportunity cost is the chairs the same slice of the week could have made: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 is the most tables the week allows. The question asks how many chairs one table replaces.
That is every chair the week could make. One table uses only its slice of the week.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting the maximums does not work. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week at a constant rate. It makes 30 chairs and 5 tables. Where does that point lie?
hints: Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.

acceptedIdeas: Inside the frontier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thirty chairs leave time for 10 tables, so 5 tables wastes capacity: the point is inside the frontier.

choices.label: Inside the frontier
On the frontier
Beyond the frontier

questions.onCorrect: Inside. 30 chairs use half the week, which could make 10 tables, so making 5 leaves time idle.

misconceptions.feedback: On the frontier means all the week is used. Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.
Beyond the frontier needs more time than the week holds. Check how much of the week 30 chairs use.

questions.prompt: Machines given up in moving from 40 to 60 food
hints: Only the machines column matters for what is given up.
Find machines at both points.
Subtract the later figure from the earlier one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall from 70 to 40: 70 − 40 = 30 machines for 20 more food.

questions.onCorrect: Machines fall from 70 to 40, so 30 machines are given up for 20 more food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines at the starting point. What is given up is the fall between the two points.
That is the machines at the end point. Take the change from start to end.
That is the food gained. The question asks about machines.

questions.prompt: On the same frontier, food rises from 60 to 80 units while machines fall from 40 to 0. What is the opportunity cost per unit of food, measured in machines?
hints: Find the machines lost on this step.
Find the food gained on this step.
Divide the loss by the gain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 machines ÷ 20 food = 2 machines per unit of food.

questions.onCorrect: 2 machines per unit. The step from 60 to 80 food costs more per unit than the step before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines lost in total. Divide by the food gained to price one unit.
That is the food gained, not the machines given up per unit.
That averages over the whole frontier. Use only the step from 60 to 80 food.

questions.prompt: Priya has 12 hours of study time. An essay takes her 3 hours and a problem set takes 1.5 hours. What is the opportunity cost of one essay, measured in problem sets?
hints: An essay uses up a fixed block of time.
Ask how many problem sets fit into that same block.
Divide the essay's time by the time for one problem set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 problem sets per essay. The 12-hour total does not change the rate.

questions.onCorrect: 2 problem sets. An essay's cost is the other task's output over the same time; the 12-hour total does not change the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many essays 12 hours allow. Compare one essay's time with one problem set's time.
That is a problem set's cost in essays, the wrong way up.
That is every problem set 12 hours could hold. One essay uses only its own block of time.

questions.prompt: A production possibilities frontier bows outward from the origin. What does that shape show?
hints: Compare how steep the frontier is near each axis.

acceptedIdeas: Increasing opportunity cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, as resources less suited to it are moved across.

choices.label: Increasing opportunity cost
Constant opportunity cost
Falling opportunity cost

questions.onCorrect: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, because resources less suited to it are moved across.

misconceptions.feedback: A constant cost gives a straight line, not a bow.
Falling cost would bend the frontier inward, towards the origin.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of one cake, in loaves?
hints: A day of cakes and a day of bread use the same time.
Ask how much bread one cake's share of the day could have made.
Divide her loaves per day by her cakes per day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 loaves ÷ 6 cakes = 2 loaves per cake.

questions.onCorrect: 2 loaves. A cake's opportunity cost is the loaves the same time could have made: 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every loaf her day could make. One cake uses only its share of the day.
That is the most cakes she can bake. The question asks how many loaves one cake replaces.
That is a loaf's cost in cakes, the wrong way up.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes; Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who gives up fewer loaves to bake a cake? Give the name.
hints: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Ana makes more cakes, but ask what each one gives up.

acceptedIdeas: Ben
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben. A cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2.

questions.onCorrect: Ben. A cake costs him 6 ÷ 4 loaves, less than Ana's 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: Ana bakes more cakes, but the question is about what she gives up. Price a cake in loaves for each baker.

questions.prompt: How many more loaves does he end with than before?
hints: Find how many loaves the swap brings him.
He keeps the same number of cakes as before.
Subtract the loaves he used to bake from the loaves he receives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He receives 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 loaves and keeps 2 cakes, so he has 3.5 − 3 = 0.5 loaves more.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5 loaves more. He keeps the same 2 cakes and ends with 3.5 loaves instead of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is all the loaves he receives. Take off the 3 he used to bake.
That is the price of one cake. He swaps two, and he already had loaves before.

questions.prompt: Cara can bake 8 loaves or 4 cakes a day; Dan can bake 4 loaves or 2 cakes. By how many loaves does their opportunity cost of a cake differ?
hints: Work out each person's loaves per cake.
Compare the two rates.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 4 ÷ 2 loaves per cake, so the costs are equal and the difference is nothing.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both give up 2 loaves per cake, so no price can leave both better off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each person's cost, not the difference between the costs.
That is how many cakes Cara can bake. Compare the loaves each gives up per cake.

questions.prompt: In an hour Mira can code 4 web pages or write 8 reports. Tom can code 1 page or write 4 reports. What is Tom's opportunity cost of one page, in reports?
hints: Use only Tom's two figures.
Ask how many reports he forgoes to spend an hour on pages.
Divide his reports per hour by his pages per hour.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tom gives up 4 reports ÷ 1 page = 4 reports per page; Mira gives up only 2.

questions.onCorrect: 4 reports. Tom's cost of a page is the reports his hour could have produced: 4 ÷ 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is pages per report, the wrong way up.
That is Mira's cost of a page. The question asks about Tom.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting does not work. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: Mira gives up 2 reports per web page; Tom gives up 4. Which division of work produces gains from trade?
hints: Give each task to the person who gives up less to do it.

acceptedIdeas: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mira has the lower opportunity cost of pages, so she codes them; Tom's lower cost of reports makes him the report writer.

choices.label: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
Tom codes pages and Mira writes reports
Each splits the hour equally

questions.onCorrect: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports: each does the job they give up less for, and both gain from trade.

misconceptions.feedback: Tom gives up more reports for each page, so he is the dearer coder. Give each job to whoever gives up less.
Splitting the hour equally ignores who is cheaper at each job. Gains come from specialising.

questions.prompt: A café's extra opening hours have marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30, and marginal costs of £30, £35, £45, £50 and £60. How many extra hours should it open?
hints: Compare benefit and cost hour by hour.
Keep adding hours while the next one brings at least as much as it costs.
Stop before the first hour whose cost exceeds its benefit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hours one to three each bring at least their cost (£90 > £30, £70 > £35, £55 > £45); the fourth brings £40 for £50.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Each of the first three brings more than it costs; later hours would bring less than they cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its own cost. Does it still pay?
Hours are added only while they pay. Look for the first one that does not.
The first hour is the best deal, but later hours can still be worth opening.

questions.prompt: Total net benefit of the three hours, in pounds
hints: The net benefit of an hour is its benefit minus its cost.
Work out the net benefit of each of those hours.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: £105. Add each hour's own net benefit.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three benefits without taking the costs off.
That adds up the costs. Net benefit is benefit minus cost.

questions.prompt: The café's hours bring marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30. Its marginal costs rise by £20 to £50, £55, £65, £70 and £80. How many extra hours should it now open?
hints: Use the new costs, hour by hour.
Compare each hour's benefit with its new cost, in order.
Count the hours whose benefit still covers the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £90 > £50 and £70 > £55, but £55 < £65, so it opens two hours.

questions.onCorrect: 2 hours. The third hour now brings less than it costs, so the stopping point moves earlier.

misconceptions.feedback: Use the new costs for every hour. Does the third still cover its own cost?
Hours are added only while they pay. Find the first one that does not.

questions.prompt: The fourth extra hour brings £40 of benefit and costs £50. By how many pounds does opening it change the café's net benefit?
hints: Subtract the hour's cost from its benefit.
Keep the sign, since a loss is negative.
Use that hour's figures only, not the averages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £40 − £50 = −£10: opening it makes the café worse off.

questions.onCorrect: −£10. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide it, so opening the fourth makes the café worse off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average benefit of four hours. Only the fourth hour's own figures decide it.
Check the sign: this hour costs more than it brings.

questions.prompt: A student values successive hours of revision at 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, and each hour costs her 25 points of other activities. How many hours should she revise?
hints: Every hour costs the same here.
Compare each hour's value with that cost in turn.
Count the hours worth more than the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50, 40 and 30 each exceed 25; the fourth hour's 20 does not.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Revise while an hour is worth more than the other activities it displaces.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its cost. Is it still worth more?
Hours count only while they are worth more than they cost. Look for the first that is not.
Every hour costs the same, so later hours can still be worth it.

questions.prompt: A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next, is called what kind of cost? One word.
hints: Think of money that has gone for good, like a non-refundable ticket.

acceptedIdeas: sunk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

questions.onCorrect: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Marginal means the extra unit. The word you want describes money already gone for good.

questions.prompt: Demand for coffee is Qd = 100 − 2P, with P in pounds and Q in cups per day. How many cups are demanded at a price of £15?
hints: Substitute the price for P.
Multiply the price by the slope first.
Subtract that product from the intercept.
questions.onCorrect: 70 cups. Multiply the price by the slope, then take the result off the intercept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 15. Take it off the intercept of 100.
That takes off the price only. Each £1 loses 2 cups.
That is the quantity at the higher price in the figure, not at £15.

questions.prompt: Equilibrium price, in pounds
hints: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.
Collect the P terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Divide the gap between the intercepts by the sum of the slopes.
questions.onCorrect: £20. Set Qd equal to Qs, collect terms and divide by the combined slope.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the combined intercepts. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the combined slope. Divide the intercepts by it.
That is the quantity traded, not the price.

questions.prompt: Cups traded per day
hints: Substitute the price into either equation.
Try the demand equation first.
Check that the supply equation gives the same number.
questions.onCorrect: 60 cups. Substitute the price into either equation; both give the same number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price. Put it into an equation to find the quantity.
That is the demand intercept. Substitute the price to find the quantity.

questions.prompt: With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20, the price is stuck at £25. How many cups are offered but not bought each day?
hints: Find quantity demanded at that price.
Find quantity supplied at that price.
Subtract demand from supply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Qs = 100 − 20 = 80 and Qd = 100 − 50 = 50, so 80 − 50 = 30 cups go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: 30 cups. At £25 sellers offer 80 and buyers want 50, so the excess goes unsold and pushes the price down.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what sellers offer. Subtract what buyers want.
That is what buyers want. Subtract it from what sellers offer.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 8 + 2P. Find the equilibrium price in pounds.
hints: Set the two quantities equal.
Move the P terms together and the constants together.
Divide the constant difference by the combined slope.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 4P = 8 + 2P gives 72 = 6P, so P = £12 and Q = 32.

questions.onCorrect: £12. Set the quantities equal, then divide the constant gap by the combined slope.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between the constants. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the quantity traded, not the price.
That is the combined slope. Divide the constants by it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 150 − 5P and supply is Qs = 30 + 10P. Find the equilibrium quantity.
hints: Find the equilibrium price first.
Set the equations equal and solve for P.
Substitute that price back into either equation.
questions.onCorrect: 110 units. Solve for the price, then substitute it back into either equation.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the equilibrium price. Substitute it to find the quantity.
That is the gap between the constants. Solve for the price first, then find the quantity.

questions.prompt: The price of coffee rises while nothing else changes. What happens on the demand diagram for coffee?
hints: Ask which variable is measured on the axis of the curve itself.

acceptedIdeas: A movement along the demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve; quantity demanded falls.

choices.label: A movement along the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.onCorrect: A movement along the curve. The good's own price is on the axis, so changing it moves buyers along the curve.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.
A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.

questions.prompt: New equilibrium price, in pounds
hints: Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the P terms on one side.
Divide the constant gap by the sum of the slopes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 150 = 6P, so P = £25, up from £20.

questions.onCorrect: £25. Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply and solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old price. Demand has shifted, so solve again with the new equation.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the quantity, not the price.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys coffee crops and sellers offer 24 fewer cups at every price: Qs = 4P − 44. Demand stays Qd = 100 − 2P. What is the new equilibrium quantity, in cups?
hints: Set the original demand equal to the new supply.
Solve for the price first.
Substitute that price into the demand equation.
questions.onCorrect: 52 cups. Supply shifted left: the price rises and the quantity falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the new price. The question asks for the quantity.
That is the old quantity. Supply has shifted, so solve again.

questions.prompt: Demand and supply each rise by 30 cups at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P and Qs = 4P + 10. By how many pounds does the equilibrium price change from its original £20?
hints: Find the new equilibrium price.
Set the new demand equal to the new supply and solve.
Subtract the old price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20, so the price is unchanged while quantity rises to 90.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both curves moved by the same amount, so quantity rose and the price stayed put.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far each curve moved, not the change in price.
That is the new quantity, not the change in price.

questions.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. The price of tea rises. What happens to the demand curve for coffee?
hints: Where might tea drinkers go when tea gets dearer?

acceptedIdeas: It shifts right.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Right: some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

choices.label: It shifts right.
It shifts left.
It does not move: this is a movement along it.

questions.onCorrect: Right. Some tea drinkers switch, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

misconceptions.feedback: Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more is wanted at each coffee price, not less.
Tea's price is not on coffee's axis, so it moves the whole curve rather than a point along it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P. A new factory adds 20 units of supply at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Write the new supply equation.
Set it equal to demand.
Solve for P.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2P; 120 − 3P = 20 + 2P gives 100 = 5P, so P = £20, down from £24.

questions.onCorrect: £20. New supply of 20 + 2P meets the unchanged demand at a lower price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price before the new factory. Solve again with the new supply.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.

questions.prompt: When the price of a concert ticket falls from £11 to £9, the number sold rises from 35 to 65. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Divide the change in quantity by the average of the two quantities.
Divide the change in price by the average of the two prices.
Divide the first percentage by the second and drop the sign.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Quantity changed by 60% of its average, price by 20% of its average: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides price by quantity. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the change in quantity, not the elasticity. Express it as a share of the average first.
Check your base: use the average of the two quantities, 50, not an end value.

questions.prompt: Ticket sales rise from 35 at £11 to 65 at £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Compute revenue at each price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue goes from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a rise of £200.

questions.onCorrect: £200 more. Elastic demand means the gain in quantity outweighs the cut in price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue before the cut. Subtract it from the revenue after.
That is the revenue after the cut. Subtract the revenue before.
That is the price cut. Revenue is price times quantity at each price.

questions.prompt: Elasticity of demand
hints: Use the average quantity as the base for the quantity change.
Use the average price as the base for the price change.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 0.25. The quantity percentage is much smaller than the price percentage, so demand is inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. The entry price falls from £11 to £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Find the quantity at each price.
Multiply each price by its quantity.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Visits rise from 90 to 110; revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after, so it does not change.

questions.onCorrect: None. Revenue is the same at both prices, which is what unit elasticity looks like.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue at one price. Compare it with the revenue at the other.
That is the price fall, not the change in revenue.

questions.prompt: Demand for a firm's product is inelastic. The firm raises its price. What happens to its total revenue?
hints: Compare the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.

acceptedIdeas: It rises
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so price times quantity goes up.

choices.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: It rises. With inelastic demand quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two percentage changes: which one is bigger when demand is inelastic?
Revenue stays level only at unit elasticity. Here quantity responds by less than price.

questions.prompt: The price of a phone case rises from £8 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 110 to 90. Find the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand.
hints: Average the two quantities and the two prices.
Express each change as a share of its average.
Divide the quantity share by the price share.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5. A 20% change in quantity against a 40% change in price: inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: A buyer would pay up to £35 for a cup of coffee and buys it at the market price of £20. How much consumer surplus does she gain, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price paid.
Start from her maximum, not from the price.
Subtract the price from her maximum.
questions.onCorrect: £15. Willingness to pay minus the price paid is the surplus on that cup.

misconceptions.feedback: That is her maximum. Surplus is the part she did not have to pay.
That is the price. Surplus is the gap between her maximum and the price.
